one_liner: Small safe-Rust, no_std WebAssembly 3.0 interpreter whose eager compile+instantiate beats every JIT runtime's startup, not WAMR's execution.
what_it_does: Embeddable WebAssembly interpreter: parse_bytes validates a module (via wasmparser) and lowers it to TinyWasm's own bytecode, ModuleInstance::instantiate places it in a Store, and typed or untyped function handles call into it. It passes the WebAssembly 3.0 core test suite (GC, exceptions, typed function references, memory64, SIMD and relaxed SIMD, tail calls), adds fuel and time-budgeted execution plus a ResourceLimiter, and can serialize parsed modules to a version-specific .twasm archive so that loading skips parsing and validation. It is not API-compatible with Wasmtime, Wasmer or WAMR; it is its own Rust API.
how_it_is_fast: The startup win is simply that it is an eager translating interpreter: it runs one validation-plus-lowering pass (single-pass since 0.11.0) into a compact internal instruction set instead of generating machine code with Cranelift, Winch or Singlepass. The bytecode uses 8-byte instructions (16 bytes before 0.11.0), separate 32/64/128-bit operand lanes and fused superinstructions (LocalCopy32/64/128, IncLocal, BinOpLocalLocal, local compare-and-branch) produced by an optimize rewrite at parse time. Dispatch is a stable-Rust match loop over the instruction enum, or, with the nightly-tail-calls feature, a handler table with explicit tail calls (become), i.e. threaded-code dispatch.
when_to_use: You need to load and run many small or short-lived Wasm modules where JIT compile time dominates: on the EPYC 7763 run it compiles+instantiates coremark in 223 us and erc20 in 212 us versus 9.87 ms and 10.00 ms for Wasmtime (Cranelift).

no_std + alloc targets, Rust code bases that forbid unsafe, or hosts where generating machine code at run time is not wanted (it is a pure interpreter and can itself compile to WebAssembly); with only the archive feature, binaries below 300 KB are claimed.
You need recent proposals in an interpreter (GC, exception handling, typed function references, memory64, relaxed SIMD) that some older small interpreters lack.
Precompiling modules ahead of time to .twasm from a trusted build step so devices skip parsing and validation on load.
when_not_to_use: Execution-heavy workloads: execution geomean on the same EPYC 7763 run is x40.50 versus WAMR fast-interpreter x17.07, Wasm3 (eager) x16.51, Wasmtime Pulley x27.92 and Wasmtime Cranelift x1.15; it is several times slower than the runtimes it beats on startup once code runs for more than a few milliseconds.

When startup latency is the only goal: lazy interpreters start much faster (Wasmi v2 lazy x1.37, Wasm3 lazy x2.77 versus Tinywasm x37.19), and V8 (x33.27) and most in-place interpreters in the same suite (DLR x10.95, Fizzy x17.83, Toywasm x18.35, SpaceWasm x25.84) also start faster.
C or C++ hosts: there is no C API yet (the changelog only mentions internal methods for a future c-api crate), unlike WAMR or Wasm3.

Untrusted .twasm archives: loading checks only the header and encoding, not Wasm validation or runtime invariants; untrusted inputs must go through the validating parser plus ParseLimits, stack, ResourceLimiter and fuel or time limits.
Projects needing WebAssembly threads or stack switching today (threads only on the unreleased next branch), or a stable API: 0.10 and 0.11 both broke the embedding API and the .twasm format.

integration.dependencies: wasmparser (parser/validation) and postcard/serde (.twasm archives) with default features; libm only with default features disabled (no_std + alloc); optional log, portable-atomic
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.98 (edition 2024) for 0.11.0; Rust 1.95 for 0.10.0; nightly Rust for the nightly-tail-calls feature
integration.platforms: any target Rust supports, including no_std and wasm32; optional simd-x86 feature for x86 SIMD intrinsics (x86-64-v3 recommended); earlier issues fixed for aarch64 build and arm32v7 panics
integration.thread_safety: Stores and store-local handles are single-threaded unless the send feature is enabled; host function definitions are Send + Sync and reusable across stores (0.11.0); shared memory and atomic wait/notify across stores only on the unreleased next branch

gotchas: The suite measured tinywasm 0.10.0 with default features (stable match-loop dispatch), not 0.11.0 with its single-pass parser, 8-byte instructions or the nightly-tail-calls backend the README recommends for maximum performance; current-release numbers may differ in either direction.

Harness detail (wasmi-benchmarks): every runtime is timed single-threaded at compile time. The Tinywasm wrapper sets parser threads to 1, and the Wasmtime wrapper builds wasmtime 47.0.0 with default-features = false, which drops Wasmtime's default parallel-compilation (rayon) feature; so the 44x gap to Wasmtime (Cranelift) is against single-threaded Cranelift and would shrink on a multi-core host with default Wasmtime. The Tinywasm wrapper also rebuilds its Store and host functions inside every timed instantiation, a small bias against Tinywasm.
Wasmtime (Pulley) is the slowest startup in the plot (x1777.72) because Pulley bytecode is produced by Cranelift; it is not a fair stand-in for a lightweight interpreter's startup.

Execution correctness history: wasmi-benchmarks' author reported Tinywasm trapping with unreachable on the compression benchmark (#47) and hanging on regex_redux (#48, closed as duplicate); 0.10.0 fixed branch stack shaping that could corrupt execution or panic, and 0.11.0 fixed memory64 bulk-memory lanes and memory.init bounds checks.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Tinywasm over Toywasm, Fizzy, SpaceWasm, DLR wasm-interpreter or Submilli-wasm when execution speed also matters (x40.50 versus x45.63 to x318.96 on the same run) and you want safe, no_std Rust with Wasm 3.0 GC and exceptions; pick Wasmi instead when you want both faster startup (lazy modes) and faster execution (x12.40) in Rust, and WAMR, Wasm3 or Silverfir-nano when execution speed or a C API matters most.
verified_claims_summary: In the Wasmi author's wasmi-benchmarks startup suite (criterion, compile plus instantiate of seven modules from erc20 to ffmpeg, single-threaded compilation, Rust bench profile with fat LTO and codegen-units 1, stable toolchain of unrecorded version) on an AMD EPYC 7763, Tinywasm 0.10.0 has a geomean of x37.19 relative to the per-case fastest runtime versus x56.73 for WAMR fast-interpreter, x298.15 for Wasmtime Winch, x1484.15 for Wasmer Cranelift and x1634.19 for Wasmtime Cranelift, roughly level with Wasmi v2 eager (x38.88) and V8 (x33.27). Per case it ranges from 212 us (erc20) to 409.56 ms (ffmpeg) versus 10.00 ms and 17.96 s for Wasmtime Cranelift.
status_note: Actively developed by one main maintainer (0.11.0 on crates.io 2026-09-19, about 25k downloads, main branch last commit 2026-09-22, next branch newer), dual MIT/Apache-2.0 and easy to add as a crate, but pre-1.0 with breaking API and .twasm changes in each minor release.
